edge.title: The phone held for ransom
edge.setup: You step out of a cab or auto and realise your phone is still on the back seat. You call it; the driver answers, agrees to return it, then names a price: 'petrol, time, risk', ₹3,000 or more, cash, now.
edge.tell: Someone returning your property who sets the price after you have shown you are desperate.
move: Stay calm and do not agree a figure; the driver's leverage is your panic, so do not show it.
Report the lost item through the ride app's support first and note the trip details, so the booking itself is the record.
If the demand stands, call 112 or go to the nearest police station with the trip details; do not hand over cash for something that is yours.
edge.why: The holder has a monopoly on one object that is worth far more to you than to them, so any price below 'give up' feels reasonable. Framing it as a favour makes refusing feel rude. Bringing a third party with a record of the trip, the app or the police, removes the monopoly and the pressure together.
edge.variants: Same shape: a 'finder' of a lost wallet asking for a reward first, a towing or parking man holding your vehicle until you pay an unofficial fee, a repair shop holding your device until an inflated bill is paid.

scenario.question: You get out of an auto near the new Pink Line station and realise your phone is on the seat. You call from a friend's phone; the driver answers, says he is already across the city, and will bring it back only for ₹3,000 in cash 'for petrol and time'. What do you do?

choices.text: Stay calm, agree no figure, note the trip details from the app, raise it with the ride app's support, and if he still demands money, call 112 or go to the nearest police station with those details.
Pay the ₹3,000 quickly, because the phone is worth far more and arguing might make him switch it off.
Haggle him down to ₹1,500 and meet him alone somewhere he chooses to hand over the cash.

lens.name: Moral hazard
lens.one_line: People take more risk when someone else carries the downside.
lens.detail: Insurance against theft reduces the care taken to prevent theft. Bailouts reduce the caution of the next lender. Deductibles, co-pays and skin-in-the-game rules exist specifically to re-link a decision to its consequence — which is why their removal, however humane it sounds, changes behaviour.
elsewhere: Limited liability encourages risk-taking — deliberately, as a feature.
A free replacement warranty subtly reduces how carefully a device is handled.
Deposit guarantees reduce depositors' scrutiny of their bank.
lens.test: Who eats the loss if this goes wrong? Whoever it is, their caution is the only caution in the system.
lens.today: The Deccan Herald warns that the Centre–state funding slugfest may cost Bengaluru Metro dearly, and The Hindu reports the Pink Line's partial opening leaves commuters wanting. When two governments share a project, each can pin a delay on the other, so neither carries the full downside; the commuter waiting for the rest of the line does. Apply the test to your own plans: if you are counting on the full line opening soon to change your commute or a house hunt, you are the one who eats the loss if it slips.
